title: Similitude 9.1: The great parable of the tower begins: twelve mountains in Arcadia
sum: Similitude 9, the longest unit of the Shepherd (78-110), opens with the Shepherd, the angel of repentance, promising to show Hermas again, and more exactly, what the Holy Spirit showed him through the Church in the Visions. He adds a startling line: "that Spirit is the Son of God" (78:1). Hermas was too weak then to see an angel; now he is strong enough (78:2-3).

The angel takes him in vision to Arcadia, sets him on a breast-shaped mountain, and shows him a great plain ringed by twelve mountains, each different: black, bare, thorny, half-dry, rough, cracked, cheerful, full of springs, desert with snakes, shady, fruitful, and white (78:4-10). The Shepherd explains them later as twelve kinds of believers from all the nations (94-106).

views.H: From here to 107:2 (Similitude 9.30.2) the only continuous Greek is the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s), which Lake calls "very inaccurate"; Sinaiticus stopped at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6). Where A skips words, Lake retranslates the Latin and Ethiopic into Greek, and this part's variants mark each place. Arcadia is in every witness, though Lake notes it "plays no further part in the story."
views.N: The thorns and thistles of the third mountain are the pair of Hebrews 6:8 and Genesis 3:18. The opening line about the Spirit and the Son invites comparison with 2 Corinthians 3:17 ("the Lord is the Spirit").
views.D: "That Spirit is the Son of God" is one of the verses that make Hermas's teaching about Christ hard to pin down. John Chapman (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910) says it has been thought "with some reason" that Hermas did not distinguish the Son from the Holy Spirit, but that "his words are not clear." See the chapter page of 89.

settings.what: The vision of the twelve mountains, the rock and gate, and the building and testing of the tower (Similitude 9)
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, who shows the vision; Hermas tells it in the first person
settings.to: Hermas, a Christian of Rome who had been a slave (1:1), alone with the angel in a vision set in Arcadia
settings.when: after Hermas had written down the Mandates and the first eight parables (78:1)
settings.why: To show again, "more exactly" (78:3), what the Church showed in Vision 3, now with the Son of God as rock, gate and lord of the tower, and with a test that exposes rotten stones. The point for Hermas is that the church is still being built, and fallen believers can still be reworked into it if they repent before it is finished (91:2).
settings.readers: Hermas's fellow Christians at Rome, the first audience the book names: he is to read it "in this city with the elders who lead the church" (8:3, Vision 2.4.3). Lake dates the book by the Muratorian list to the time Pius was bishop, "about 148," while "many critics" think it "may have been written at intervals during the twenty or thirty years preceding."

title: Similitude 9.2: The white rock, the new gate and the twelve virgins
sum: In the middle of the plain stands a great white rock, square and higher than the mountains, big enough to hold the whole world. It is old, but a gate has been newly cut into it, and the gate shines brighter than the sun (79:1-2). Twelve virgins in linen tunics stand around the gate, four at the corners and two between each, right shoulders bare, ready to carry loads (79:3-4).

Hermas is amazed and puzzled that such delicate women stand as if to carry the whole sky. The Shepherd scolds him gently: do not strain after what you cannot see; ask the Lord, master what is in front of you, and wait for the explanation (79:5-7).

views.H: The Amherst papyrus, one of the papyrus fragments Lake lists, holds parts of 79:1-2 and 79:4-5, where it adds a "were" that A lacks (79:4). Lake's footnote pictures the gate as "a sort of porch, cut out of the rock," with the tower built directly above it.
views.N: The rock and gate will be the Son of God (89:1), as Christ is "the rock" in 1 Corinthians 10:4 and "the door" in John 10:9. The square shape recalls the city that "lies in a square" (Revelation 21:16).
views.J: The Shepherd's advice not to pry into what is too hard echoes Sirach: "Do not go looking for things harder than you can handle" (Sirach 3:21).
views.D: The virgins, explained in 90:2 as holy spirits and powers of the Son, are not saints or angels but virtues. Five of their names are those of the seven women of Vision 3 (16:7).

title: Similitude 9.3: Six men, the builders and the ten stones from the deep
sum: Six tall, glorious men arrive and summon a crowd of strong builders to raise a tower above the rock. The virgins urge them to hurry and hold out their hands (80:1-2). At the six men's command ten square, bright stones rise from a deep place, uncut, and the virgins carry them through the gate to the builders (80:3-5).
The scene repeats Vision 3, where six young men built the tower with stones from the deep (10:5). Here the rule is added that every stone must pass through the gate in the virgins' hands.

views.H: A, the Ethiopic and the Latin all say the ten stones were "cut" (Lake's footnote names these three); Lake adds "not" because 82:3 calls them uncut. The site follows Lake and marks it as his correction.
views.N: The church as a building raised by God's agents, with Christ as its base, is the picture of Ephesians 2:20-22 and 1 Peter 2:5.
views.J: Angels as builders and attendants fit the Jewish picture of God's heavenly court; the Shepherd later names the six as glorious angels (89:8).

title: Similitude 9.4: The foundation rows and the stones from the mountains
sum: The virgins carry the stones in their standing formation, the strongest at the corners (81:1). The ten stones fill the rock and become the foundation; the rock and gate bear the whole tower (81:2). Twenty, thirty-five and forty more stones rise from the deep and make four rows of foundation (81:3).

Then the builders bring stones of many colors from the twelve mountains. Those carried through the gate by the virgins turn white; those the men set in themselves stay as they were, look out of place, and are taken back down. "Do not wear yourselves out for nothing" (81:4-8).

views.H: The witnesses disagree on the second row: twenty (A, Lake), twenty-five (Latin), fifteen (Ethiopic). Two phrases here are Lake's Greek retranslated from the Latin and Ethiopic, because A skips them.
views.N: "No one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid" (1 Corinthians 3:11). Ephesians 2:20 puts apostles and prophets in the foundation; so does Hermas (92:4).
views.D: Only stones carried by the virgins through the gate change color: belonging to the church outwardly is not enough without the Son (the gate) and the virtues (the virgins). The explanation comes in 90:2-9.

title: Similitude 9.5: A pause in the building
sum: The day's work ends, but the tower is not complete: more is to be built on, so there is a pause. The builders rest; the virgins stay to guard the tower (82:1). The tower cannot be finished, the Shepherd says, until its lord comes to test it and replace rotten stones (82:2).

Hermas pours out his questions about the rock, gate, mountains, virgins and the numbers of the stones, and asks for rest for his soul. If he is not idly curious, he will learn everything. A few days later they return, for the tower's owner is coming to inspect it (82:3-7).

views.H: Hermas's question gives the numbers as ten, twenty, thirty-five and forty, matching A at 81:3. A copyist's slip of the eye in A drops the promise in 82:5, which Lake restores from the versions.
views.N: The lord who comes to test the building recalls 1 Corinthians 3:13 ("the fire itself will test") and Malachi 3:1. The pause is the forbearance of Romans 2:4 and 3:25.
views.D: The pause is the time for repentance (91:2), the book's main theme: there is still room for sinners, but not forever.

title: Similitude 9.6: The lord of the tower tests the stones
sum: A procession arrives, and in its middle a man taller than the tower, with the six men at his sides and many glorious beings around him. The virgins run to kiss him and walk with him around the tower (83:1-2). He feels every stone and strikes each with a rod; some turn black, scabby, cracked, chipped, neither white nor black, rough, or stained. These rotten stones are taken out (83:3-5).

Replacements come not from the mountains but from a nearby plain: bright square stones, which are cut and set in, and round ones, too hard to cut quickly, which are laid beside the tower to be cut later because they are so bright (83:6-8).

views.H: Three passages in this chapter are Lake's Greek put back from the Latin and Ethiopic; A also adds "three times" to the striking, which Lake leaves out with L and E.
views.N: The great figure among angels who sorts the good from the bad recalls the Son of Man who comes "along with the holy angels" (Mark 8:38; Matthew 25:31). The round stones are the rich (107:4-5), Hermas's version of Mark 10:25.
views.D: The test exposes believers who are inside the church but have gone bad. The book does not treat them as lost: in the next chapter they are handed to the angel of repentance.
views.R: Hermas speaks often to the rich in Rome's church (the elm and the vine, 51, Similitude 2); the bright round stones that must be trimmed before they fit speak to them.

title: Similitude 9.7: The rejected stones handed to the Shepherd
sum: The glorious man, lord of the whole tower, hands the rejected stones to the Shepherd: clean them, fit back in those that can fit, and throw the rest far away. He leaves with his company, and the virgins stand guard (84:1-3).

Hermas asks how rejected stones can return. The Shepherd says he will cut most of them; the small will go in the middle and the large outside to hold them. They must clean everything before the master comes suddenly and finds dirt, "and I will look careless in the master's eyes" (84:4-7).

views.H: The lord's departure (84:3) is missing in A and restored by Lake from the versions.
views.N: "Rejected" is the word of Psalm 118:22 and 1 Peter 2:7, here turned from Christ to believers. The master who may come suddenly is the master of Jesus' parables (Mark 13:36; Matthew 24:50).
views.D: This is the book's doctrine of repentance in picture: the Son of God judges, but hands the fallen to the angel of repentance to be reworked, not destroyed. Lake calls the book "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance"; how churches read it is set out at 31 (Mandate 4.3).

title: Similitude 9.8: Sorting the rejected stones
sum: The Shepherd works through the rejected stones kind by kind. The black ones are unchanged and set apart. Of the scabby, cracked, chipped, half-white, rough and stained stones, some prove black or too damaged and are thrown out; the rest are cut and fitted back by the virgins (85:1-7).
Where they go depends on strength: the weaker go into the middle of the building, the sound ones on the outside "because of their strength," so that they can hold the others in.

views.H: One small variant: the Latin's "sound" against A's "those" (85:7). Lake's English footnote explains "weaker": "i.e. to endure the strain of the outside."
views.N: The strong placed to protect the weak recalls Romans 15:1 and Galatians 6:2.
views.D: The chapter shows the book's realism: not every fallen believer returns, but many do, and those who return are given a place that fits what they can bear.

title: Similitude 9.9: The round stones, the women in black, and the tower like one stone
sum: Last come the white round stones. Hermas confesses he is no stonecutter. The Shepherd cuts the larger and brighter ones and sets them on the outside; the rest go back to the plain, not rejected, because a little more remains to be built and the master wants them all (86:1-4).

Twelve beautiful women in black, hair loose and shoulders bare, "savage" to look at, cheerfully carry the rejected stones back to the mountains (86:5-6). The finished tower is so well built that it looks like one stone carved from the rock (86:7).

views.H: Part of 86:5 is Lake's Greek put back from the Latin and the Ethiopic. In 86:4 Lake reads A as "all," though the letters are hard to read, where the Latin's "perhaps" seems to him to stand for "surely."
views.N: The seamless tower is the "one body" of Ephesians 4:4, explained in 90:5.
views.J: The women in black recall the seductive woman of Proverbs 7, who is beautiful and dangerous; in 90:8 they "talk" believers into sin.
views.D: The rich (the round stones) are neither rejected nor admitted as they are: there is still room for them, once their wealth is cut back (107:4-5).

title: Similitude 9.10: The ground made clean, and Hermas left with the virgins
sum: The Shepherd has Hermas bring lime and fine bits of pottery to fill the holes left by the stones and level the ground; the virgins sweep away the dung and sprinkle water, and the place becomes cheerful and beautiful (87:1-3). All is ready for the lord's visit.

When the Shepherd tries to leave, Hermas grabs his bag and begs him by the Lord to explain everything. The Shepherd promises to return and puts Hermas in the virgins' care. Left alone with them, Hermas finds them even more cheerful and kind, especially the four greatest (87:4-7).

views.H: Lake's footnote on the "marks" of the stones: "Apparently the meaning is that the holes left in the ground where stones had been taken out were to be filled up and levelled."
views.N: The Shepherd's bag (pēra) is the one he wore when he first came (25:1), the bag Jesus told the Twelve not to take (Matthew 10:10).

settings.what: Hermas left in the virgins' care for a night
settings.by: The virgins, speaking to Hermas, and the Shepherd on his return
settings.to: Hermas, who wants to go home and is ashamed to stay
settings.when: while the Shepherd is away, through an evening and a night beside the tower
settings.why: The virgins, who stand for the virtues (92:2), keep Hermas with them "as a brother and not as a husband" and spend the night in prayer. The scene shows Hermas living among the virtues before he learns their names, and the Shepherd's questions at his return ("Did they treat you well?") show that it went as it should.
settings.readers: Hermas's fellow Christians in Rome, many of whom, like him, had to learn the virtues after a fall (91:3). The book's first readers knew the Visions' warnings about desire (1:8), so the chaste night is pointed.

title: Similitude 9.11: A night of prayer with the virgins
sum: The virgins tell Hermas the Shepherd will not come today and refuse to let him go home: he was put in their care. He will sleep among them "as a brother and not as a husband," for they love him and will live with him from now on. Hermas is ashamed (88:1-3).

They kiss him, lead him around the tower, and dance and sing; Hermas walks silently with them and feels young again (88:4-5). At night they spread their linen tunics on the ground, lay him in the middle, and do nothing but pray, and he prays with them without stopping until morning (88:6-7). When the Shepherd returns, Hermas says he "supped on words of the Lord all night," and asks to hear everything in order (88:8-9).

views.N: The meal of the Lord's words recalls Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4. Paul's advice to treat younger women "as sisters, keeping yourself entirely pure" (1 Timothy 5:2) is the spirit of the scene.
views.D: The scene is plainly chaste: the virgins call Hermas their brother and the night is prayer. Because they are virtues, many read it as the Christian living with the virtues; the site's note at 88:5 gives Claude's own theory that it acts out being "clothed" by them (90:2).
views.J: Like other apocalypses, Hermas uses an everyday scene (hospitality, a meal, a night's lodging) to carry a lesson, and the host's question "What did you have for supper?" is answered with the Lord's words.

readings: The virgins are the virtues (92:2). Hermas spends a night among them in prayer, grows young, and is fed with the Lord's words: the life the explanation describes (90:2-5; 91:3) is shown before it is explained.

Hermas is shy and human: ashamed to stay, silent while the others dance, glad in the morning. The Shepherd's teasing questions ("You have not done him any harm, have you?") lighten a long and serious parable.

title: Similitude 9.12: The rock and the gate are the Son of God
sum: The explanation begins. The rock and the gate are the Son of God. The rock is old because the Son is "older than all his creation," the Father's counselor in it; the gate is new because he "appeared in the last days," so that those who are saved may enter the kingdom of God through it (89:1-3). No one enters the kingdom without receiving his name, just as no one enters a walled city except by its one gate (89:4-5).

The builders are glorious angels, a wall around the Lord, and even they come to him only through the Son. The glorious man who walked around the tower and rejected stones is the Son of God, with six glorious angels at his right and left (89:6-8).

views.H: The Amherst papyrus holds 89:2-3 and 89:5 and gives "the rock is old" where A has "he is old" (the form Lightfoot quotes). Lake's margin cites Proverbs 8:27-30 at 89:2 and John 3:5 and 14:6 at 89:3-6.
views.N: Christ as the only way (John 14:6; Acts 4:12), made known "at the completion of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26) and "in the last of the times" (1 Peter 1:20); the Son through whom and for whom creation was made (Colossians 1:15-17; John 1:3).
views.J: The Son as the Father's counselor before creation is told in the language of Wisdom at God's side (Proverbs 8:27-30; Wisdom of Solomon 9:9). In 58:3 (Similitude 5.5.3) the Lord's counselors are angels; here the Son alone.
views.D: This chapter is the core of the question of Hermas's Christology: a Son who existed before creation (Lightfoot), a Son not clearly told apart from the Spirit (Chapman, as a view he reports and does not adopt), and Lake's judgment that the Christology is "very hard to reconstruct." See the deep sections below.

echoes: Proverbs 8:22-31; John 1:1-3; John 10:9; John 14:6; Colossians 1:15-17; Hebrews 1:2-3; Hebrews 9:26; 1 Peter 1:20; Acts 4:12; 1 Corinthians 10:4

deep.h: Rock, gate, glorious man: what Hermas says
deep.b: Three pictures in this chapter are all "the Son of God": the rock that is older than all creation, because the Son was "the Father's counselor for his creation" (89:2); the gate, new because "he appeared in the last days, at the completion of the age" (89:3), the one way into the kingdom (89:4-6); and the glorious man, taller than the tower, who tests it and is attended by six angels (89:7-8). Add 78:1, "that Spirit is the Son of God," and 91:5, his name "holds up the whole world." Hermas never writes "Jesus" or "Christ" in these chapters, and he never explains how these pictures fit together. Christians have read him in several ways.

deep.h: A Son who existed before creation
deep.b: J. B. Lightfoot (Galatians, 1874 printing, pp. 324-325) answered those who called Hermas an Ebionite, that is, one who held Jesus to be only a man. He quotes 89:1-3 and cites 91:5, and concludes: "Such expressions no Ebionite could have used." On this reading the old rock is the Son before the world, and the new gate is the same Son who appeared in the last days, so Hermas holds pre-existence and incarnation together, in his own pictures.

deep.h: A Son not clearly distinguished from the Spirit
deep.b: John Chapman, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), notes that "It has been thought with some reason that he did not distinguish the Son from the Holy Ghost" or "that the Holy Ghost became the Son by His Incarnation,". Chapman cites no verses; on this site the ones that bear on it are 78:1 and 59:5-7 (Similitude 5.6.5-7), where God makes the Holy Spirit dwell in flesh. The second reading he reports would make the Son become Son at the incarnation, the question the chapter page of 59 takes up. Chapman's own judgment: "his words are not clear, and his ideas on the subject may have been rather misty and confused than definitely erroneous."

deep.h: Is the Son pictured as an angel?
deep.b: In 69:3 (Similitude 8.3.3) the great and glorious angel is Michael; here "the glorious man" is the Son of God, flanked by "glorious angels." Lake's footnote on Michael at 69:3 notes the clash, "But in Sim. ix. he is the Son of God," and says that this, together with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit, "makes it very hard to reconstruct the Christology of Hermas." Lake names the difficulty and does not propose an answer, and no source opened for this page argues that Hermas made the Son an angel. So the site gives the question, not a holder: the verses that raise it are 69:3 and 89:7-8; against it, 89:8 says no glorious angel comes to God without him, and 89:2 puts him before all creation.

deep.h: How the churches have read it
deep.b: How the churches received the Shepherd itself, read in church by some and set aside by others, is set out on the book's page. The sources opened for this chapter are an editor (Lake), a historian of doctrine (Lightfoot) and an encyclopedia article (Chapman), not church documents ruling on these verses, so there is no "Where Christians differ" card here. The question is historical: what a Roman Christian of the second century or a little before (the date is disputed: see the book page) could say about the Son before the councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) gave the church its fixed words. The site's notes at 78:1, 89:2 and 89:8 give the evidence verse by verse.

deep.title: Claude's theory: one Son, old rock and new gate
deep.b: Hermas answers the question "how can the rock be old and the gate new?" by making both pictures one thing: rock and gate "are the Son of God" (89:1), with one verb in the Greek, esti, "is." The singular verb may be no more than grammar; the theory rests on the images. He may be using the two pictures to say what later theology said with two words, before and after: the same Son is eternal (old rock) and has appeared in time (new gate), without explaining how. This is Claude's reading of the images; it overlaps with Lightfoot's use of 89:1-3 against an Ebionite reading, but goes beyond what Lightfoot says.

deep.title: Claude's theory: six angels and the Son make seven
deep.b: The six glorious angels with the Son between them make a company of seven. Jewish writings on the site know seven chief angels: Raphael is "one of the seven angels who stand in attendance" (Tobit 12:15), 1 Enoch 20 lists seven holy angels by name, and Revelation has "the seven angels who stand in God's presence" (Revelation 8:2). Hermas does not say this, and he keeps the Son apart ("none of these glorious angels will come in to God without him"). If the echo is real, the picture puts the Son at the center of heaven's highest court, which is part of why readers ask whether Hermas thought of him as an angel. This is Claude's suggestion only.

settings.what: The Shepherd's explanation of the parable, begun here and continued through 110
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, who asks one question at a time, in the order of the vision (88:9)
settings.when: the morning after the night with the virgins, at the tower
settings.why: To turn the pictures into teaching: the Son of God is the church's foundation and only way in; the virtues must clothe those who bear his name; the fallen can return through repentance while the building pauses. Each answer meets a question Hermas has asked, so the reader learns as he does.
settings.readers: The same Roman church, now given the key to the pictures. The Shepherd's answers speak to believers who had received the name in baptism and fallen (90:6-9), the readers Hermas counts himself among when he thanks God for sending the angel of repentance "to us who had sinned" (91:3).

title: Similitude 9.13: The tower is the church; the virgins are holy spirits
sum: The tower, the Shepherd says, is the church (90:1). The virgins are holy spirits, powers of the Son of God; no one enters the kingdom unless they clothe him in their garment, and bearing the name without their power is useless (90:2). Their names are their clothing, and the Son himself bears them (90:3). That is why the tower became one stone with the rock: believers who put on these spirits become "one spirit, one body," all one color (90:4-5).

The rejected stones had received both the name and the virgins' power and lived as one with God's slaves, but later the beautiful women in black talked them into desiring them; they put on the women's power, took off the virgins', and were thrown out of the house of God (90:6-9).

views.H: Two passages rest on the versions: 90:4 is partly Lake's Greek put back from the Latin and Ethiopic, and in 90:8 the Vulgate Latin has "garment" where A and the Palatine Latin have "power."
views.N: Lake's margin: "one body and one Spirit" (Ephesians 4:4); "think the same way" (Philippians 2:2). Being clothed with virtues echoes Colossians 3:12-14 and Galatians 3:27.
views.J: The seductive women recall Proverbs 7, and the house of God the temple language Israel used of God's people.
views.D: Hermas separates receiving the name (baptism, 93:3-4) from wearing the virtues. Those who fall away had truly received both, so the book speaks to believers who lose what they had, the problem it was written to address.

echoes: 11:3; Ephesians 2:20-22; Ephesians 4:4; Colossians 3:12-14; Galatians 3:27; 1 Timothy 3:15; Proverbs 7:21; 1 Peter 2:5

title: Similitude 9.14: Room for repentance, and the name that holds up the world
sum: Can the rejected return? Yes, if they throw off the women's works, take up the virgins' power again, and walk in it: "That is the very reason the building had a pause." If they do not repent, others will take their place, and they will be thrown out for good (91:1-2). Hermas gives thanks that the Lord had compassion on those called by his name and sent the angel of repentance to "us who had sinned" (91:3).

Why is the tower built on the rock and gate? Because the Son's name is great, cannot be contained, and holds up the whole world; if he holds up all creation, he will hold up those who bear his name with their whole heart and are not ashamed of it. He became their foundation (91:4-6).

views.H: A has "others will go in" where L and E have "will enter"; the sense is the same. Lake translates 91:3 "all who call upon his name," but his margin cites Isaiah 43:7.
views.N: The Son who holds up the world is the Son of Hebrews 1:3 and Colossians 1:17. The warning of Hebrews 6:4-6 stands behind the book's question whether the fallen can repent; Hermas answers yes, while time remains.
views.D: This chapter puts in a picture what Lake calls the book's message: forgiveness for sin after baptism for those who repent, "though this repentance would not avail more than once." The rule is given at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6), where the site sets out how churches have read it.
views.J: "Called by his name" is the Bible's language for God's people (Isaiah 43:7; compare James 2:7).

echoes: Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:17; Isaiah 43:7; James 2:7; Mark 8:38; Romans 1:16; 31:6

title: Similitude 9.15: The names of the virgins and the women, and the stones from the deep
sum: The four strong virgins at the corners are Faith, Self-control, Power and Patience; the eight between are Simplicity, Innocence, Purity, Cheerfulness, Truth, Discernment, Harmony and Love. Whoever bears these names and the Son's name will enter the kingdom (92:1-2). The women in black: four stronger, Unbelief, Lack of Self-control, Disobedience and Deceit, followed by Grief, Wickedness, Shameless Living, Bad Temper, Lying, Foolishness, Slander and Hatred. A slave of God who bears these will see the kingdom but not enter it (92:3).

The stones from the deep: the ten are the first generation, the twenty-five the second generation of righteous people, the thirty-five God's prophets and servants, the forty apostles and teachers of the preaching of the Son of God (92:4). The virgins carried them because they were the first to bear these spirits and kept them until they fell asleep (92:5-6).

views.H: The opening question is restored by Lake from the versions, because A's copyist skipped from one "of the virgins" to the next. The number of the second row is twenty-five here but twenty in 81:3 and 82:4; Lake: the numbers "do not quite agree," and "no satisfactory hypothesis has ever been suggested."
views.N: The virtues overlap Paul's fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23) and 2 Peter 1:5-7; the vices overlap the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:19-21). "See but not enter" recalls Moses at Deuteronomy 34:4 (Lake's margin).
views.J: Faith opening and Love closing a chain of virtues is already in Vision 3 (16:7). Lists of virtues and vices were a common teaching form among Jews and Christians alike (compare Wisdom of Solomon 8:7 and the Two Ways of the Didache).
views.D: The foundation rows set God's prophets and his servants beside the apostles and teachers of the Son. Hermas gives no names or dates for the first two "generations"; reading them as the righteous of Israel's early history is Claude's inference from their place before the prophets. In 93 the apostles preach to the dead and give them the seal, a passage read alongside 1 Peter 3:19.
